title: Salvation came to this house (Luke 19:1–10)
hookLine: Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays four times over

lines: TODAY I MUST ABIDE AT THY HOUSE.
cards: Still in Jericho. The first half of this story is the part with the tree: a short, rich chief tax collector named Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore to see over the crowd, and Jesus stops underneath and calls him by name.

"Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Today we follow them inside, because what Zacchaeus says at his own table, with the town grumbling outside, is a speech nobody asked for.
Luke records no sermon from Jesus first. Zacchaeus just stands up.

teach.b: First the grumbling. They all murmured, "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." Zacchaeus is a chief among the tax collectors, and rich; to the crowd, that made him a sinner.
Then he stands and says, in the King James Bible: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold."
Here's why fourfold is striking. The law of Moses had rules for paying back what you'd taken. For many wrongs, you returned it and added a fifth.
But for a stolen sheep, Exodus says: "he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep." Zacchaeus reaches past the added fifth to the sheep thief's penalty. Nobody told him to.

Jesus never mentioned money. Being welcomed did what lectures hadn't. A few scholars point out that the Greek verbs are present tense, I give, I restore, and wonder if he's describing what he already does.
Others read a new promise, there and then. Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham." This day.
Luke comes back to that word at big moments: the angels at his birth, born this day; Nazareth, this day this scripture is fulfilled; and on the cross, today again.

teach.h: THIS DAY IS SALVATION COME TO THIS HOUSE.
teach.b: Salvation in Luke isn't only someday. It walks into a house, sits down to dinner, and changes how the money moves.

how: The story of Zacchaeus is read when Christians talk about repentance that changes behavior; Catholic and Orthodox teaching count making restitution as part of turning back after a wrong, and in the Roman Rite the story is read at the dedication of a church.

games.q: you're Zacchaeus. Jesus is at your table, and you can hear the whole town grumbling outside. what do you do?
o: defend yourself: tax collecting is legal.
stand up and promise half to the poor and fourfold to anyone you cheated.
say nothing and enjoy the honor.
games.why: "the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold."

practice: Think of one thing you owe someone, money forgotten, a favor never returned, credit that was really theirs, without spiraling into guilt. Imagine paying it back not exactly but generously, more than you owe, the way Zacchaeus did.
If you pray, give thanks for being welcomed first.

wordCard.voice: Zacchaeus, the short, rich chief tax collector who climbed a tree to see Jesus, then gave half to the poor and repaid fourfold.

orig.note: Greek: today, this day. a word Luke returns to, from the angels' song to the cross.

carryVoice: Your line: today, salvation. Not someday: this day, at a dinner table. See you tomorrow.
